lines.say: Lesson 1: What is a Medical Claim?

lines.raw: Every doctor visit leaves a paper trail.
lines.say: Every doctor visit leaves a paper trail.

lines.raw: That trail is a medical claim.
lines.say: That trail is a medical claim.

lines.raw: In this lesson you will:
lines.say: In this lesson you will:

lines.raw: Explain in one sentence what a medical claim is.
lines.say: Explain in one sentence what a medical claim is.

lines.raw: Know who creates a claim, who sends it, and who pays it.
lines.say: Know who creates a claim, who sends it, and who pays it.

lines.raw: Name the six questions every claim answers.
lines.say: Name the six questions every claim answers.

lines.raw: Tell a claim apart from an encounter and a medical record.
lines.say: Tell a claim apart from an encounter and a medical record.

lines.raw: Start with something you already know.
lines.say: Start with something you already know.

scenes.section: Start with something you already know

lines.raw: Think about the last time you or someone in your family went to a hospital in Nepal.
lines.say: Think about the last time you or someone in your family went to a hospital in Nepal.

lines.raw: You probably got an **OPD ticket**, the doctor wrote on a **prescription paper**, you paid for **tests** at the counter, and you walked out with a **bill** (receipt).
lines.say: You probably got an O P D ticket, the doctor wrote on a prescription paper, you paid for tests at the counter, and you walked out with a bill (receipt).

scenes.section: Start with something you already know

lines.raw: That bill quietly records a lot: **who** was treated, **which doctor** saw them, **what** was done, **when** it happened, and **how much** it cost.
lines.say: That bill quietly records a lot: who was treated, which doctor saw them, what was done, when it happened, and how much it cost.

lines.raw: In the US, that same information is collected in a standard format and sent to an insurance company.
lines.say: In the U S, that same information is collected in a standard format and sent to an insurance company.

lines.raw: That bill is called a **medical claim**, and a pile of them is what people call **medical data**.
lines.say: That bill is called a medical claim, and a pile of them is what people call medical data.

scenes.section: Start with something you already know

lines.raw: Simple definition.
lines.say: Simple definition.

lines.raw: A medical claim is a bill that a doctor or hospital sends to an insurance company, asking to be paid for care they gave, written in a way the insurance company can read and pay.
lines.say: A medical claim is a bill that a doctor or hospital sends to an insurance company, asking to be paid for care they gave, written in a way the insurance company can read and pay.

lines.raw: Meet our three people.
lines.say: Meet our three people.

lines.raw: Throughout this course we will follow three people with the same kind of problem, so you can compare how things work.
lines.say: Throughout this course we will follow three people with the same kind of problem, so you can compare how things work.

lines.raw: In Nepal: Sita and Ram both get sick in Kathmandu.
lines.say: In Nepal: Sita and Ram both get sick in Kathmandu.

lines.raw: With private insurance:
lines.say: With private insurance:

lines.raw: **Ram** works at a tech startup.
lines.say: Ram works at a tech startup.

lines.raw: The startup is not in SSF, but it gives Ram **private health insurance** from an insurance company.
lines.say: The startup is not in S S F, but it gives Ram private health insurance from an insurance company.

lines.raw: He visits a hospital with a sore throat and fever.
lines.say: He visits a hospital with a sore throat and fever.

lines.raw: He buys an OPD ticket, sees the doctor, pays for a blood test, and buys medicine.
lines.say: He buys an O P D ticket, sees the doctor, pays for a blood test, and buys medicine.

lines.raw: He **pays the whole bill himself** at the counter and keeps the original bills, prescription and reports.
lines.say: He pays the whole bill himself at the counter and keeps the original bills, prescription and reports.

lines.raw: Later, he **submits a claim** with those papers to his insurance company.
lines.say: Later, he submits a claim with those papers to his insurance company.

lines.raw: The insurer checks it and **reimburses** (pays back) Ram.
lines.say: The insurer checks it and reimburses (pays back) Ram.

lines.raw: With the Social Security Fund:
lines.say: With the Social Security Fund:

lines.raw: **Sita** is an accountant at a private company.
lines.say: Sita is an accountant at a private company.

lines.raw: Every month, part of her salary goes to the **Social Security Fund (SSF)**.
lines.say: Every month, part of her salary goes to the Social Security Fund (S S F).

lines.raw: She visits an **SSF-listed hospital** with the same sore throat.
lines.say: She visits an S S F listed hospital with the same sore throat.

lines.raw: She shows her SSF ID card.
lines.say: She shows her S S F I D card.

lines.raw: The hospital treats her.
lines.say: The hospital treats her.

lines.raw: Sita pays **20%** of the bill herself at the hospital.
lines.say: Sita pays 20 percent of the bill herself at the hospital.

lines.raw: This is called **cost sharing**.
lines.say: This is called cost sharing.

lines.raw: The hospital then **sends the bill to SSF** for the other **80%**.
lines.say: The hospital then sends the bill to S S F for the other 80 percent.

lines.raw: SSF checks it and pays the hospital.
lines.say: S S F checks it and pays the hospital.

lines.raw: In the US: Emily gets sick in Texas, USA.
lines.say: In the U S: Emily gets sick in Texas, U S A.

lines.raw: **Emily** works at a company that gives her **health insurance** (an "employer plan").
lines.say: Emily works at a company that gives her health insurance (an "employer plan").

lines.raw: She visits her doctor with a sore throat.
lines.say: She visits her doctor with a sore throat.

lines.raw: She shows her insurance card at the front desk.
lines.say: She shows her insurance card at the front desk.

lines.raw: After the visit, the doctor's office **sends a bill to her insurance company**.
lines.say: After the visit, the doctor's office sends a bill to her insurance company.

lines.raw: That bill is called a **claim**.
lines.say: That bill is called a claim.

lines.raw: The insurance company checks it, pays its share, and tells Emily what she still owes.
lines.say: The insurance company checks it, pays its share, and tells Emily what she still owes.

lines.raw: The big idea.
lines.say: The big idea.

lines.raw: Both Sita and Ram create a **claim**, just in different ways.
lines.say: Both Sita and Ram create a claim, just in different ways.

lines.raw: With SSF, the **hospital** sends the claim and gets paid directly.
lines.say: With S S F, the hospital sends the claim and gets paid directly.

lines.raw: That is how most US visits work.
lines.say: That is how most U S visits work.

lines.raw: With Ram's private insurance, **Ram** pays first and sends the claim himself to get his money back.
lines.say: With Ram's private insurance, Ram pays first and sends the claim himself to get his money back.

lines.raw: That happens in the US too, usually when a patient sees a doctor outside their insurer's network.
lines.say: That happens in the U S too, usually when a patient sees a doctor outside their insurer's network.

lines.raw: Even Sita's 20% share has a US twin: Emily also pays part of each bill herself.
lines.say: Even Sita's 20 percent share has a U S twin: Emily also pays part of each bill herself.

lines.raw: Who is involved?
lines.say: Who is involved?

lines.raw: The same roles in three situations.
lines.say: The same roles in three situations.

lines.raw: Patient. Ram (Nepal, private insurance): Ram (policyholder). Sita (Nepal, SSF): Sita (SSF contributor). Emily (USA): Emily (called a **member**).
lines.say: Patient. Ram (Nepal, private insurance): Ram (policyholder). Sita (Nepal, S S F): Sita (S S F contributor). Emily (U S A): Emily (called a member).

lines.raw: Provider (who gives care). Ram (Nepal, private insurance): Any hospital & doctor. Sita (Nepal, SSF): SSF-listed hospital & doctor. Emily (USA): Doctor's office or hospital.
lines.say: Provider (who gives care). Ram (Nepal, private insurance): Any hospital and doctor. Sita (Nepal, S S F): S S F listed hospital and doctor. Emily (U S A): Doctor's office or hospital.

lines.raw: Payer (who pays the bill). Ram (Nepal, private insurance): Ram pays first, then his insurer pays him back. Sita (Nepal, SSF): SSF pays 80%, Sita pays 20%. Emily (USA): Insurance company (the **payer**), Emily pays a share.
lines.say: Payer (who pays the bill). Ram (Nepal, private insurance): Ram pays first, then his insurer pays him back. Sita (Nepal, S S F): S S F pays 80 percent, Sita pays 20 percent. Emily (U S A): Insurance company (the payer), Emily pays a share.

lines.raw: Who sends the claim? Ram (Nepal, private insurance): **Ram** (to his insurer). Sita (Nepal, SSF): The **hospital** (to SSF). Emily (USA): The **doctor or hospital** (to the insurer).
lines.say: Who sends the claim? Ram (Nepal, private insurance): Ram (to his insurer). Sita (Nepal, S S F): The hospital (to S S F). Emily (U S A): The doctor or hospital (to the insurer).

lines.raw: A claim is a bill with a story.
lines.say: A claim is a bill with a story.

scenes.section: A claim is a bill with a story

lines.raw: A claim is more than a number.
lines.say: A claim is more than a number.

lines.raw: It tells the full story of the visit by answering six questions.
lines.say: It tells the full story of the visit by answering six questions.

lines.raw: Each later lesson in this course explains one of them.
lines.say: Each later lesson in this course explains one of them.

scenes.section: A claim is a bill with a story

lines.raw: Here is a quick table.
lines.say: Here is a quick table.

lines.raw: **Why?**. What the claim records: The health problem (diagnosis). Emily's example: Strep throat. Lesson: 5.
lines.say: Why?. What the claim records: The health problem (diagnosis). Emily's example: Strep throat. Lesson: 5.

lines.raw: **What?**. What the claim records: Services and procedures done. Emily's example: Office visit + strep throat test. Lesson: 6.
lines.say: What?. What the claim records: Services and procedures done. Emily's example: Office visit and strep throat test. Lesson: 6.

lines.raw: **When?**. What the claim records: The date(s) of service. Emily's example: 10 March 2025. Lesson: 7.
lines.say: When?. What the claim records: The date(s) of service. Emily's example: 10 March 2025. Lesson: 7.

lines.raw: **Who?**. What the claim records: The patient, and the doctor or hospital who treated them. Emily's example: Emily Carter, seen by Dr. Patel. Lesson: 8.
lines.say: Who?. What the claim records: The patient, and the doctor or hospital who treated them. Emily's example: Emily Carter, seen by Doctor Patel. Lesson: 8.

lines.raw: **Where?**. What the claim records: The place care happened. Emily's example: Doctor's office. Lesson: 9.
lines.say: Where?. What the claim records: The place care happened. Emily's example: Doctor's office. Lesson: 9.

lines.raw: **How much?**. What the claim records: The amount charged, and later, what was paid. Emily's example: $150 charged. Lesson: 10.
lines.say: How much?. What the claim records: The amount charged, and later, what was paid. Emily's example: 150 dollars charged. Lesson: 10.

scenes.section: A claim is a bill with a story

lines.raw: Remember: Who, What, Where, When, Why, How much.
lines.say: Remember: Who, What, Where, When, Why, How much.

lines.raw: If you remember these six questions, you understand the shape of every medical claim.
lines.say: If you remember these six questions, you understand the shape of every medical claim.

lines.raw: Lessons 2 to 4 first show how a claim is laid out; lessons 5 to 10 then fill in one question each.
lines.say: Lessons 2 to 4 first show how a claim is laid out; lessons 5 to 10 then fill in one question each.

lines.raw: Claim vs. encounter vs. medical record.
lines.say: Claim versus encounter versus medical record.

lines.raw: Three kinds of records describe the same visit.
lines.say: Three kinds of records describe the same visit.

lines.raw: Only one of them is a bill.
lines.say: Only one of them is a bill.

scenes.section: Claim vs. encounter vs. medical record

lines.raw: Claim.
lines.say: Claim.

lines.raw: A bill sent for payment.
lines.say: A bill sent for payment.

lines.raw: Contains codes and money.
lines.say: Contains codes and money.

lines.raw: Encounter.
lines.say: Encounter.

lines.raw: A record of a visit sent for reporting, even when no separate payment is needed (for example, when a doctor is already paid a fixed monthly amount).
lines.say: A record of a visit sent for reporting, even when no separate payment is needed (for example, when a doctor is already paid a fixed monthly amount).

lines.raw: Looks almost like a claim.
lines.say: Looks almost like a claim.

lines.raw: Medical record (EMR / EHR).
lines.say: Medical record (E M R or E H R).

lines.raw: The doctor's detailed notes about the patient (Electronic Medical / Health Record).
lines.say: The doctor's detailed notes about the patient (Electronic Medical or Health Record).

lines.raw: Like the full patient file kept at the hospital in Nepal.
lines.say: Like the full patient file kept at the hospital in Nepal.

lines.raw: It stays with the provider and is not sent as a bill.
lines.say: It stays with the provider and is not sent as a bill.

lines.say: Medical claims are one of several data types.

lines.say: An insurance company receives many kinds of data.

scenes.section: Medical claims are one of several data types

lines.raw: Here is a quick table.
lines.say: Here is a quick table.

lines.raw: **Eligibility**. What it tells you: Who is covered, and from which date to which date. Nepal comparison: Is Sita's SSF contribution up to date?
lines.say: Eligibility. What it tells you: Who is covered, and from which date to which date. Nepal comparison: Is Sita's S S F contribution up to date?

lines.raw: **Medical**. What it tells you: Doctor and hospital services. Nepal comparison: OPD, admission, surgery bills.
lines.say: Medical. What it tells you: Doctor and hospital services. Nepal comparison: O P D, admission, surgery bills.

lines.raw: **Pharmacy**. What it tells you: Medicines bought with a prescription. Nepal comparison: Bill from the medical shop / pharmacy.
lines.say: Pharmacy. What it tells you: Medicines bought with a prescription. Nepal comparison: Bill from the medical shop or pharmacy.

lines.raw: **Lab**. What it tells you: Test results (sugar level, cholesterol). Nepal comparison: The lab report you collect the next day.
lines.say: Lab. What it tells you: Test results (sugar level, cholesterol). Nepal comparison: The lab report you collect the next day.

lines.raw: **Biometrics**. What it tells you: Height, weight, blood pressure. Nepal comparison: Numbers written on your OPD card.
lines.say: Biometrics. What it tells you: Height, weight, blood pressure. Nepal comparison: Numbers written on your O P D card.

lines.raw: How big is US healthcare?
lines.say: How big is U S healthcare?

lines.raw: Very big.
lines.say: Very big.

lines.raw: Most of this money moves through claims, which is why claims data matters so much.
lines.say: Most of this money moves through claims, which is why claims data matters so much.

lines.raw: US health spending in 2023 (source: CMS, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, the US government's health agency).
lines.say: U S health spending in 2023 (source: C M S, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, the U S government's health agency).

lines.raw: Total spent in one year. Amount: **$4.9 trillion**. To picture it: More than **100 times** Nepal's entire economy (about $40 billion a year).
lines.say: Total spent in one year. Amount: 4.9 trillion dollars. To picture it: More than 100 times Nepal's entire economy (about 40 billion dollars a year).

lines.raw: Share of the US economy. Amount: **17.6%**. To picture it: About **$1 of every $6** spent in the US goes to healthcare.
lines.say: Share of the U S economy. Amount: 17.6 percent. To picture it: About 1 dollar of every 6 dollars spent in the U S goes to healthcare.

lines.raw: Spent per person. Amount: **$14,570**. To picture it: Roughly **Rs 20 lakh** per person, every year.
lines.say: Spent per person. Amount: 14570 dollars. To picture it: Roughly Rs 20 lakh per person, every year.

lines.raw: Hospital care alone. Amount: **$1.5 trillion**. To picture it: The largest single piece, about 3 of every 10 dollars.
lines.say: Hospital care alone. Amount: 1.5 trillion dollars. To picture it: The largest single piece, about 3 of every 10 dollars.

lines.raw: Doctor and clinic services. Amount: **$978 billion**. To picture it: About 2 of every 10 dollars.
lines.say: Doctor and clinic services. Amount: 978 billion dollars. To picture it: About 2 of every 10 dollars.

lines.raw: Why this matters for data.
lines.say: Why this matters for data.

lines.raw: Insurers, employers and data companies use medical claims to pay bills correctly, catch fraud, find people who need extra care, and measure whether care is good.
lines.say: Insurers, employers and data companies use medical claims to pay bills correctly, catch fraud, find people who need extra care, and measure whether care is good.

lines.raw: When so much money moves through claims, even a tiny error rate is huge: a mistake in just **1%** of US health spending is about **$49 billion**.
lines.say: When so much money moves through claims, even a tiny error rate is huge: a mistake in just 1 percent of U S health spending is about 49 billion dollars.

lines.raw: If you work with US healthcare data, medical claims will be the biggest table you touch.
lines.say: If you work with U S healthcare data, medical claims will be the biggest table you touch.

lines.raw: Key takeaways.
lines.say: Key takeaways.

lines.raw: A medical claim is the bill a doctor or hospital sends to an insurance company for care it gave.
lines.say: A medical claim is the bill a doctor or hospital sends to an insurance company for care it gave.

lines.raw: Nepal's SSF works the same way as most US visits: the hospital sends the claim.
lines.say: Nepal's S S F works the same way as most U S visits: the hospital sends the claim.

lines.raw: Ram's private insurance works by **reimbursement**: he pays first, then claims the money back.
lines.say: Ram's private insurance works by reimbursement: he pays first, then claims the money back.

lines.raw: Every claim answers six questions: Who, What, Where, When, Why and How much.
lines.say: Every claim answers six questions: Who, What, Where, When, Why and How much.

lines.raw: A claim is a bill; an encounter reports a visit without asking for separate payment; a medical record is the doctor's notes.
lines.say: A claim is a bill; an encounter reports a visit without asking for separate payment; a medical record is the doctor's notes.

lines.raw: Medical is one data type.
lines.say: Medical is one data type.

lines.raw: Others include eligibility, pharmacy, lab and biometrics.
lines.say: Others include eligibility, pharmacy, lab and biometrics.
